title: Hardware, Computer Systems, GPU Architecture, CUDA, and RHI
abstract: A systems-to-graphics guide connecting CPU, memory, flash, buses, processes, pages, threads, locks, GPU execution, CUDA, RHI design, and the practical differences among OpenGL, Direct3D 11, Direct3D 12, and Vulkan.
image: /content/blog/Hardware, Computer Systems, GPU Architecture, CUDA, and RHI/hardware-system-rhi.svg
imageAlt: A CPU and memory hierarchy feed a GPU through an interconnect, then branch into OpenGL, Direct3D, Vulkan, and an engine RHI
lede: Rendering performance starts below the renderer. CPU scheduling, memory locality, storage, interconnects, operating-system isolation, GPU hierarchy, and API submission all determine when useful work reaches the device. This guide preserves the supplied vocabulary—including Cuda and Valkan—while identifying the official names CUDA and Vulkan, adding the missing architectural terms, and separating current AI-systems research from deterministic hardware, OS, and graphics-API contracts.

sections.heading: Computer system: compute, memory, storage, and interconnect
paragraphs: A computer system is a hierarchy, not a single processor. The CPU executes instructions, caches keep recent data close, DRAM holds the active working set, flash-backed storage preserves data without power, and buses or coherent fabrics move commands and bytes between components.

Performance follows the slowest required path. A fast CPU can still wait on cache misses, page faults, storage reads, or transfers to an accelerator. Latency describes how long one operation takes; bandwidth describes how much data can move per unit time; concurrency is needed to hide one with useful work from another.

terms: Small transfers are latency-bound; large transfers approach the link's sustainable bandwidth.

equations.label: Amdahl's law
terms: p is the parallel fraction and N the available parallel resources.

sections.heading: Process, page, thread, and synchronization
paragraphs: The operating system turns hardware into isolated execution contexts. A process owns a virtual address space and resources; threads are schedulable execution streams that can share that process state; pages are the granularity by which virtual addresses are mapped and protected.

Multithreading introduces communication through shared memory. Locks create critical sections, atomics create indivisible operations with explicit ordering, and condition variables or futexes let a thread sleep instead of spinning. Correctness requires a happens-before relation; performance additionally requires low contention and cache-friendly ownership.

sections.heading: GPU structure: throughput from hierarchical parallelism
paragraphs: A GPU trades single-thread latency for aggregate throughput. Many streaming multiprocessors or compute units schedule groups of lightweight lanes, keep thousands of threads resident, and switch among ready warps or wavefronts while other groups wait for memory or functional units.

The memory hierarchy is part of the execution model. Registers and shared memory are fast but limited and determine occupancy; global VRAM is large but expensive; coalesced access and tiled reuse convert bandwidth into useful work. Divergent control flow and uncoalesced traffic waste lanes and transactions.

sections.heading: CUDA: mapping kernels onto NVIDIA GPUs
paragraphs: CUDA is NVIDIA's platform and programming model for general-purpose GPU computing. Host code launches a kernel over a grid of thread blocks; hardware schedules blocks independently onto SMs; each block is divided into warps; threads cooperate through block-local memory and synchronization.

Correct CUDA code must respect scope. A block barrier does not synchronize another block, a stream orders only its own submitted work unless dependencies connect streams, and host–device transfers are not automatically free. PTX is a virtual ISA used in compilation, not a promise that source maps one-to-one onto machine instructions.

sections.heading: RHI and graphics APIs: OpenGL, Direct3D 11/12, and Vulkan
paragraphs: A Render Hardware Interface (RHI) is an engine-owned abstraction over platform graphics APIs. It gives the renderer common resource, pipeline, command, synchronization, and presentation concepts while each backend translates them to OpenGL, Direct3D, Vulkan, Metal, or console-specific calls.

The main divide is responsibility. OpenGL and Direct3D 11 let the driver infer and validate more state; Direct3D 12 and Vulkan expose command recording, resource states, memory allocation, descriptors, queues, and synchronization more explicitly. Explicit APIs can reduce driver overhead and scale command generation, but move lifetime and hazard bugs into engine code.

aiResearch.summary: KernelBench and Astra test LLM-generated CUDA kernels, while HipKittens develops a cross-vendor tile abstraction for AMD AI kernels. This work sits beside the graphics RHI: it targets compute-kernel authoring and portability, not learned OpenGL, Direct3D, or Vulkan synchronization rules.

closing: A frame crosses several ownership boundaries: process and threads organize CPU work; pages and caches decide where its data resides; buses move resources to a throughput-oriented GPU; CUDA exposes NVIDIA compute hierarchy; an RHI translates engine intent into one graphics API's resource and synchronization model. OpenGL and Direct3D 11 keep more responsibility in the driver, while Direct3D 12 and Vulkan return more control—and more proof obligations—to the engine.
